title: Nothing Eats Alone
principle: All those lines together are called a food web.

t: Draw a line from a thing to the thing that eats it. Keep going. You will not get a chain — you will get a mess.
Start with one species and draw an arrow to whatever eats it, then repeat. What you get is never a tidy chain, and the untidiness is the important part.
sub: The neat food chain in most textbooks is a simplification that removes the property that matters.

question: Which is safer for a fox: eating only rabbits, or eating five different things?
Which strategy is more robust: specialising on one prey species, or generalising across several?
options: Five different things — one bad year does not finish it
Only rabbits — it gets very good at catching them
stages.outcome: Five different things — one bad year does not finish it
note: Commit. Note that the specialist really is better at its one job, which is what makes this a trade-off rather than an obvious answer.

t: Put each thing where it belongs in the web.
Every organism occupies a position defined by what it eats and what eats it. Place them.

label: Makes its own food from light
Producer: fixes energy from sunlight
Eats the ones that make food
Primary consumer: eats producers
Eats the ones that eat plants
Secondary consumer: eats primary consumers
Eats whatever has died, and gives it back
Decomposer: returns nutrients to the producers

t: All those lines together are called a food web.
The whole network of who-eats-what is a food web. A food chain is one thread pulled out of it.
A food web is the full set of trophic links. The chain is a useful abstraction that discards exactly the property — redundancy — that determines how the system responds to loss.

Which is why chains mislead. A chain implies that removing a link breaks everything downstream; a web implies that it usually does not, because there are other routes. Whether a particular removal matters is then an empirical question about that web's structure rather than something readable off a diagram.
sub: And the decomposers are the part everyone forgets.
Every web closes: decomposers return the material to the producers, so nutrients cycle even though energy does not.
That distinction is the one to hold — energy flows through and is lost, matter goes round.

Without decomposition the nutrients would all end up locked in dead material within a few decades and productivity would stop. It is the least visible part of every ecosystem and the one whose removal would be fastest to matter.

q: Why is a food web safer than a food chain?
Why does a web tolerate a loss that a chain would not?
What property does the chain abstraction discard?
options: If one link goes, there are other routes
Webs have more animals in them
Chains only exist in the sea
why: In a chain, if one thing disappears everything above it goes hungry. In a web there is usually something else to eat, so losing one link does not have to bring the whole thing down.
Redundancy. Multiple routes to the same energy mean the loss of one link can be absorbed — which is why real ecosystems survive losses that a chain diagram predicts would be fatal.

It discards redundancy, which is the property that determines robustness. That makes the chain actively misleading rather than merely simplified: it predicts fragility that is usually absent, and it gives no way to identify the cases — keystone species — where the fragility is real.

t: It is why a specialist animal is usually the first to be in trouble.

Species that eat one thing are efficient and exposed. Pandas, koalas and many specialist insects are threatened partly because a single failure in their one food source has no alternative route — while generalists like foxes and crows thrive nearly everywhere. Diet breadth predicts extinction risk about as well as any single trait.
